## Introduction

- Recall that ANOVA allows us to compare the means of three or more groups.

- In one-way ANOVA, we are only considering one factor (grouping variable). 

- On Monday, we discussed two-way ANOVA, which allows us to consider a second factor (grouping variable). 

- Today, we are discussing profile plots and posthoc tests in the two-way ANOVA setting.

## `R` Setup 

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(ssstats)

supplement_heart_rate <- read_csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/samanthaseals/STA4173Fa26/refs/heads/main/lectures/data/supplement_heart_rate.csv") 
exercise_recovery <- read_csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/samanthaseals/STA4173Fa26/refs/heads/main/lectures/data/exercise_recovery.csv") 
```

## Two-Way ANOVA: Profile Plots

- We can construct profile plots to display treatment group means.

    - *y*-axis: always the average outcome
    
    - *x*-axis: either factor A or B
    
    - "lines" on the plot: the factor that was not selected for the *x*-axis

- Note that this is just a graph of the means! 

    - It's valid to construct a profile plot regardless of significance.
    
## Two-Way ANOVA: Profile Plots (R)

- We will use the `profile_plot()` function from `library(ssstats)` to construct basic profile plots.

```{r}
#| eval: false
dataset_name |> profile_plot(continuous = continuous_variable,
                              xaxis = variable_on_x,
                              lines = variable_for_lines)
```    

## Example 1

- Fluttershy asks: "Does the supplement affect every pony type in the same way?"

- We used the `supplement_heart_rate` dataset to determine if the effect of treatment on resting heart rate depends on pony type.

```{r}
#| echo: false

supplement_heart_rate |> head(n=3)
```

## Example 1

- We want to work towards a profile plot. The first question we ask is what levels are in each variable?

```{r}
supplement_heart_rate |> count(pony_type)
supplement_heart_rate |> count(treatment)
```

## Example 1

- Neither variable has natural ordering.

    - Treatment: placebo, supplement
    - Pony type: earth, pegasus, unicorn
    
- My choice would be: 

    - put pony type on the *x*-axis 
    - create lines for treatment
    
- Why? 

    - When there is no ordering, we then move to thinking about how many lines will be created. 
    
    - It will be much easier to draw conclusions with fewer lines (graph is less busy).

## Example 1

- Constructing the profile plot,

```{r}
#| fig-align: 'center'
supplement_heart_rate |> profile_plot(outcome = resting_heart_rate_bpm,
                              xaxis = pony_type,
                              lines = treatment)
``` 

## Example 1

- What does it look like if we switch `xaxis` and `lines`?

```{r}
#| fig-align: 'center'
supplement_heart_rate |> profile_plot(outcome = resting_heart_rate_bpm,
                              xaxis = treatment,
                              lines = pony_type)
``` 

## Example 2

- Twilight Sparkle asks: "Can the Ponyville clinic help ponies recover faster after exercise? Does the treatment work the same way across pony types?"

- We used the `exercise_recovery` to test whether the effect of recovery treatment depends on pony type.

```{r}
#| echo: false
exercise_recovery |> head(n=3)
```

## Example 2

- What levels are in each variable?

```{r}
exercise_recovery |> count(treatment)
exercise_recovery |> count(pony_type)
```

## Example 2

- Neither variable has natural ordering.

    - Treatment: enhanced, new, standard
    - Pony type: earth, pegasus, unicorn
    
- My choice would be: 

    - put treatment on the *x*-axis 
    
        - impose ordering: standard, new, enhanced
        
    - create lines for pony type

```{r}
exercise_recovery <- exercise_recovery |>
  mutate(treatment = factor(treatment,
                            levels = c("Standard care", "New treatment", "Enhanced treatment")))
```

## Example 2

- Constructing the profile plot,

```{r}
#| fig-align: 'center'
exercise_recovery |> profile_plot(outcome = recovery_time_min,
                              xaxis = treatment,
                              lines = pony_type)
``` 

## Example 2

- What if we switch the *x*-axis and the lines?

```{r}
#| fig-align: 'center'
exercise_recovery |> profile_plot(outcome = recovery_time_min,
                              xaxis = pony_type,
                              lines = treatment)
``` 

## Posthoc Testing

- Recall our hypotheses for main effects,

    - $H_0: \mu_1 = \mu_2 = ... = \mu_a$
    - $H_1:$ at least one $\mu_i$ is different
    
- We will again turn to posthoc tests to determine pairwise differences.

- Tying this to the profile plot, posthoc tests are giving us the $p$-values corresponding to pairwise differences.

## Posthoc Testing (`R`)

- We will again use the `posthoc()` function,

```{r}
#| eval: false
dataset_name |> posthoc(outcome = response_variable,
                        A = factor_A,
                        B = factor_B,
                        interaction = TRUE or FALSE,
                        adjust = TRUE or FALSE)
```

## Example 1

- Fluttershy asks: "Does the supplement affect every pony type in the same way?"

- We used the `supplement_heart_rate` dataset to determine if the effect of treatment on resting heart rate depends on pony type.

```{r}
supplement_heart_rate |> anovas(outcome = resting_heart_rate_bpm,
                                A = pony_type,
                                B = treatment)
```

## Example 1

- We can look at the posthoc test of the interaction term.

- Treating it as confirmatory,

```{r}
supplement_heart_rate |> posthoc(outcome = resting_heart_rate_bpm,
                                 A = pony_type,
                                 B = treatment,
                                 adjust = TRUE)
```

## Example 2

- Twilight Sparkle asks: "Can the Ponyville clinic help ponies recover faster after exercise? Does the treatment work the same way across pony types?"

- We used the `exercise_recovery` to test whether the effect of recovery treatment depends on pony type.

```{r}
exercise_recovery |> anovas(outcome = recovery_time_min,
                            A = pony_type,
                            B = treatment)
```

## Example 2

- Twilight Sparkle asks: "Can the Ponyville clinic help ponies recover faster after exercise? Does the treatment work the same way across pony types?"

- We then removed the (non-significant) interaction term,

```{r}
exercise_recovery |> anovas(outcome = recovery_time_min,
                            A = pony_type,
                            B = treatment,
                            interaction = FALSE)
```

## Example 2

- We now look at the posthoc test for *only* `treatment`

    - We did not detect a difference between the pony types ($p = 0.530$).

- Treating it as exploratory,

```{r}
exercise_recovery |> posthoc(outcome = recovery_time_min,
                             A = pony_type,
                             B = treatment,
                             interaction = FALSE,
                             adjust = FALSE)
```

## Wrap Up

- In this lecture, we have covered posthoc testing and profile plots in two-way ANOVA.

    - Interactions.
    
    - Main effects.
    
- We can tie the results from posthoc testing to the profile plot.

    - The profile plot is allowing us to visualize the differences between factors or treatment groups.
